mcqs.question: Why is "no shared mutable state" a complete concurrency answer for a truly immutable object?
options: Because immutable objects run their reads on a separate garbage collector thread
Because immutability makes reads faster than writes, sidestepping races entirely
Because no thread can observe a partial update when nothing about the object changes after construction — there's nothing to race on
Because the JVM automatically synchronizes access to any field marked final
mcqs.explanation: A race requires a mutation another thread could observe mid-flight; a genuinely immutable object never mutates after construction, so there's nothing to race on. There's no separate GC thread involved, no automatic final-field synchronization, and speed isn't the mechanism at work.

mcqs.question: Why does naive immutability break down for the 10-million-entry ImmutableIndex example?
options: Because Map.copyOf throws an exception once a map exceeds a fixed size limit
Because immutable collections cannot hold more than a few thousand entries in Java
Because large immutable objects require an explicit Lock to construct, unlike small ones
Because reconstructing the entire structure on every update costs O(n) time and memory, which stops being cheap at scale
mcqs.explanation: Map.copyOf has no size limit and throws no such exception, and immutable collections handle arbitrarily large sizes fine — the real cost is that a full-copy rebuild on every update is O(n), which is fine at a dozen entries and expensive at ten million.

mcqs.question: A class has only final fields, but one is a `final List<String>` whose contents can still be mutated by an external caller holding the same reference. Is the class truly immutable?
options: No — final only prevents reassigning the field, not mutating the object it references, so the class is not truly immutable
Yes — any field declared final automatically makes the whole object immutable
Yes, as long as the field is private, regardless of what it references
No, but only because a List is used instead of an array
mcqs.explanation: final only stops the field from being reassigned to a different object; it says nothing about the mutability of the object the field already points to. Privacy alone doesn't fix this if the constructor or a getter still exposes the same mutable reference, and the same issue applies to arrays too.

mcqs.question: Why isn't "immutable objects never need any synchronization" completely true?
options: Immutable state itself can be mutated once the JIT compiler optimizes the class
Publishing the reference to another thread still needs a safe-publication guarantee — a reader can otherwise observe a stale or partially-constructed reference
Immutable objects always require a final method modifier to prevent subclassing races
Java's garbage collector is not thread-safe specifically for immutable objects
mcqs.explanation: Immutability protects the object's content, not the act of handing its reference to another thread — without safe publication, a reader can see a stale or half-built reference due to reordering. The JIT never makes immutable state mutable, and neither claim about method modifiers or the garbage collector is real.
